Summary: Is green growth possible?
- Short answer: Yes—deep, sustained economic growth while sharply cutting emissions is technically feasible and is already occurring in parts of the economy, but only under strong, coordinated policy and structural change; present decarbonization rates in many advanced economies are still too slow to meet 1.5–2 °C targets while maintaining historical growth rates, so green growth pathways require faster power-sector decarbonization, electrification, circularity, and industrial process innovation, alongside robust carbon pricing and standards, and careful management of trade-offs and distributional issues. <cite id="67040153-0">Empirical studies show some high‑income countries have achieved absolute decoupling of emissions and GDP in the past decade, but current decoupling rates are insufficient to meet 1.5 °C fair‑share pathways while continuing historical GDP growth; for example, the UK would need to more than triple its decoupling rate by 2025 and accelerate it almost fivefold by 2030 to enable green growth consistent with a 1.5 °C budget</cite> <cite id="67040153-1">At the same time, observed subnational production decoupling remains inadequate for net‑zero by 2050, and scenarios that deliver green growth rely on rapid expansion of emissions‑free or negative‑emissions energy</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-3">Recent assessments find we are on a lower‑emissions trajectory than often assumed but are still off‑track for 1.5 °C or below 2 °C, implying that without faster mitigation, warming will be 2–3 °C by 2100</cite>.

What “green growth” means and what has been observed
- Definition and distinction: Green growth hinges on decoupling environmental pressures from economic activity. Evidence is strong for relative decoupling (emissions per unit of GDP down), but absolute decoupling (total emissions fall while GDP grows) has been rare and is the hard, contested target. <cite id="67040153-4">Theoretically, decoupling is possible; empirically, there is clear evidence for relative decoupling but not for absolute decoupling at national or global scales</cite> <cite id="67040153-3">Reviews conclude absolute long‑term decoupling of GDP and CO2 is rare; even when countries show decoupling in GDP–CO2, net resource/ material decoupling is not evident, and scholars argue 1.5–2 °C targets may not be feasible under continued growth without degrowth strategies</cite>.
- Real‑world achievements: Subnational jurisdictions and some advanced economies demonstrate partial/absolute decoupling in practice, often via energy intensity improvements, power sector decarbonization, and electrification. <cite id="67040153-1">Subnational action is crucial; in the US, subnational action alone could reduce national emissions by a quarter to a third, and many cities and regions have set independent net‑zero targets</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Model‑based assessments show absolute decoupling tendencies for highly industrialized economies (US, Germany, EU) under “climate‑active” baselines, though their per‑capita footprints remain high and global decoupling remains relative due to fast‑catching Asian economies</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">In Israel, GDP is projected to grow ~140% by 2050 under baseline, with energy‑related GHGs rising ~35%; with strong policy mixes, emissions can be reduced 40% (standards) to 67% (carbon pricing) relative to 2015, with power generation rising as electrification and solar scale</cite>.

How much faster must decarbonization proceed?
- Quantified gaps: Cross‑country analyses indicate current decoupling rates in advanced economies are inconsistent with fair‑share budgets under continued GDP growth. <cite id="67040153-0">Between 2013–2019, high‑income countries achieved decoupling but at rates far short of what is required to respect 1.5 °C carbon‑budget shares while maintaining historical GDP growth; the UK would need to increase its decoupling rate to 17.4% by 2025 (up from 5.3% per year) and to 23.9% by 2030—an acceleration by ~3–5×</cite>. 
- Global plausibility windows: Scenario frameworks from IPCC and modeling consortia show that low‑emission futures exist, but they require rapid, sustained mitigation beyond current policies. <cite id="9eb9de65-1">IPCC AR6 recognizes that scenarios with very high emissions (SSP5‑8.5/RCP8.5) are less likely, while low‑emission pathways (SSP1‑1.9) keep warming around 1.5 °C, reflecting feasibility of low‑growth or decoupled trajectories</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-3">A subset of plausible IPCC/IEA‑consistent scenarios projects 2–3 °C warming by 2100 with continued mitigation progress, indicating we are on a lower‑emissions path than commonly feared but still off‑track for 1.5/2 °C</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-0">Global cost‑optimal scenarios used by multiple IAMs underpin feasible pathways to below 1.5–2 °C when combined with socio‑economic assumptions across demographics, development, policy, technology, and natural resources</cite>.

Policy bundles that make green growth feasible
- Carbon pricing plus technology/standards: Deep cuts alongside continued GDP growth are achievable where carbon pricing is credible and paired with sectoral standards. <cite id="67040153-2">In Israel, a carbon tax alone reduces energy‑related GHGs by 67% versus baseline by 2050; technology standards add ~5% more reduction and induce higher power generation as transport electrifies and solar rises to ~65–85% of the mix in scenarios</cite>.
- Power sector decarbonization and electrification: The main engine of absolute decoupling in advanced economies. <cite id="58c13877-4">Decomposition shows that improvements in electricity intensity and shifts away from thermal generation were key drivers of emissions reductions in the US and Germany</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">EU, Germany, and the US exhibit absolute decoupling tendencies under climate‑active baselines, with strong reductions in per‑capita CO2 footprints while GDP grows</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">Electrification of transport and large shares of solar in the power mix are central to enabling GDP growth without emissions increases in high‑income contexts</cite>.
- Circular economy and material efficiency: Reducing material throughput is necessary to complement energy/efficiency decoupling. <cite id="58c13877-3">Model‑based assessments find that while advanced economies can achieve absolute decoupling tendencies, material footprint decoupling is weaker on average; China’s infrastructure investment dynamics drive relative global trends</cite> <cite id="67040153-3">Evidence reviews emphasize that effective resource use and emissions reduction are necessary for green growth, while absolute decoupling of GDP and material use remains rare; degrowth may be required where resource constraints bind</cite>.
- Trade‑offs and distribution: Green growth is not a free lunch; it involves short‑term costs and distributional challenges that can be addressed through just transition policies. <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Scholarship highlights that feasibility is multidimensional and that limited‑GDP‑energy growth pathways can reduce climate feasibility concerns, though they entail trade‑offs in social justice and energy system upskilling</cite>.

Constraints, critiques, and risks to feasibility
- Absolute vs relative decoupling and offshoring: Many economies have reduced emissions per unit GDP but not total emissions; trade and supply chains shift impacts without policy. <cite id="67040153-4">Evidence shows relative, not absolute, decoupling; offshoring and reliance on efficiency alone are major limits</cite> <cite id="67040153-3">Global reviews report no evidence of national/international net resource decoupling; dematerialization has not kept pace with GDP</cite>.
- Catch‑up dynamics in emerging economies: Rapid industrialization and infrastructure investment can keep material and emissions growth in lockstep with GDP, limiting global absolute decoupling. <cite id="58c13877-3">China’s surge in infrastructure investment sustains higher material footprints; relative global decoupling persists as Asian economies dominate material use growth</cite>.
- Rebound and behavioral limits: Even with efficiency gains, demand can rebound; technological progress often targets intensity rather than absolute throughput. <cite id="67040153-4">Critiques note that efficiency improvements are insufficient to reduce material throughput, and dematerialization has not materialized at scale</cite>.
- Scenario plausibility: Even with aggressive mitigation, plausible pathways still imply 2–3 °C without additional constraints, underscoring urgency. <cite id="9eb9de65-3">Plausible IPCC/IEA‑consistent scenarios project 2–3 °C by 2100 unless mitigation accelerates beyond current trajectories</cite>.

When is green growth “possible”?
- Technically possible with rapid, coordinated policy: Scenarios and case evidence show that sustained GDP growth with deep emissions cuts is feasible where carbon and non‑carbon prices internalize damages, where power supply rapidly decarbonizes, and where industry adopts process/technological innovations and circular practices. <cite id="67040153-1">Green growth is already embedded in many mitigation scenarios that project rising GDP with falling emissions via emission‑free or negative‑emissions energy</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">National case analysis demonstrates that GDP can grow while emissions are cut deeply when standards and carbon pricing are implemented</cite>.
- Politically and institutionally challenging: Feasibility depends on credible policy design and delivery across borders and supply chains. <cite id="67040153-0">Current decoupling rates in high‑income countries fall short of 1.5 °C fair‑shares at current GDP growth rates, implying policy must accelerate several‑fold within a decade</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Scholars argue mainstream IAMs may understate feasibility constraints, and lower‑growth pathways can reduce reliance on absolute decoupling and speed up renewable scaling</cite>.
- Resource and supply‑chain considerations: Critical minerals and manufacturing capacity for renewables/batteries/CCUS are bottlenecks that must be addressed in national industrial strategies. <cite id="58c13877-3">China’s dominance in infrastructure‑driven material footprints highlights the need to manage supply‑chain dependencies and accelerate raw‑material efficiency to enable global absolute decoupling</cite>.

What would make green growth more likely (conditions and steps)
- Price carbon comprehensively and credibly: High, rising carbon prices across fuels and products, paired with robust enforcement. <cite id="67040153-2">Carbon pricing alone can deliver −67% energy‑related GHG reductions versus baseline by 2050 in Israel, with sectoral standards adding further cuts</cite>.
- Electrify end‑uses and decarbonize power: Rapid expansion of variable renewables, grid modernization, long‑lived storage, and grid resilience; electrify transport, buildings, industry heat. <cite id="67040153-2">Electrification of transport and large solar shares in power mixes emerge endogenously in deep‑mitigation scenarios</cite> <cite id="58c13877-4">Improvements in electricity intensity and reductions in thermal generation share are key drivers of emissions reductions</cite>.
- Industrial decarbonization and circular economy: Process innovation, green steel/ hydrogen, CCUS where needed, industrial heat electrification, and circular design/lifecycle management. <cite id="58c13877-2">Manufacturing sector studies show large potential from technical progress and energy‑saving technologies; China’s scenarios suggest cost savings of $12–$35 billion by 2050 through CCS or hydrogen with energy efficiency</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Raw material intensity must decline to enable absolute decoupling at national level</cite>.
- Manage supply chains and trade: Address carbon leakage and embedded emissions via border‑adjustment and international standards; invest in clean supply‑chain capacity. <cite id="67040153-1">Subnational jurisdictions can materially cut national emissions, yet national policies remain essential to meet net‑zero targets</cite>.
- Finance and just transition: Redirect capital toward green assets; support workforce and community transitions. <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Limited GDP/energy growth pathways can reduce feasibility concerns of rapid mitigation but require careful attention to social and institutional feasibility</cite>.
- Monitor, audit, and adapt: Track absolute consumption‑based emissions, material footprints, and progress by geography and sector; close efficiency and offshoring gaps. <cite id="67040153-4">Accounting for offshored emissions is essential to assess true environmental impacts</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Decomposition of Kaya‑style identities highlights where to target efficiency, intensity, and structural change</cite>.

Bottom line
- Green growth is possible—economically, technically, and empirically—where policy creates strong price signals, invests in clean energy systems, and drives industrial and circular economy transformations. <cite id="67040153-1">Many mitigation scenarios assume GDP growth alongside emissions declines via emission‑free or negative‑emissions energy</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">National modeling shows GDP growth can proceed with emissions falling sharply when standards and carbon pricing are implemented</cite>. However, present trajectories in advanced economies are insufficient; without accelerating decarbonization several‑fold over the next decade, global warming will exceed 2 °C. <cite id="67040153-0">High‑income countries’ realized decoupling rates are far below what is needed to meet 1.5 °C fair‑share budgets while maintaining historical GDP growth</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-3">Plausible IPCC/IEA‑consistent scenarios project 2–3 °C by 2100 unless mitigation accelerates</cite>. Making green growth the default, not an aspiration, requires credible carbon pricing, rapid power‑sector decarbonization, industrial process innovation, circular strategies, and governance that manages distributional and supply‑chain risks—conditions that are increasingly within reach but demand urgent, coordinated action. <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Scholarly debates emphasize feasibility is multidimensional and that limiting GDP/energy growth can reduce reliance on absolute decoupling and ease the pace of renewable upscaling</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Advanced economies can show absolute decoupling tendencies, but global absolute decoupling remains constrained by fast‑catching material use in Asia</cite>.

Uncertainties and where evidence is thin
- The magnitude of rebound effects and consumer behavior shifts varies by context and technology; better empirical identification is needed to calibrate policy packages. <cite id="67040153-4">Efficiency‑only strategies and service‑based economies are not sufficient to reduce material throughput</cite>.
- Critical mineral bottlenecks and geopolitical risks for clean tech supply chains remain under‑modeled in some national scenarios; more integrated supply‑chain and industrial policy evidence is needed. <cite id="58c13877-3">China’s infrastructure‑driven material footprints illustrate the sensitivity of decoupling to investment dynamics and supply‑chain control</cite>.
- Distributional impacts and social license for rapid transitions (e.g., grid reconfiguration, industrial restructuring) require more research and inclusive governance. <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Institutional and sociocultural feasibility concerns are not yet quantified and must be addressed for just transitions</cite>.

Practical takeaway
- For a given economy, ask: Do we have rising carbon prices, a rapid clean power build‑out, electrification at end‑uses, industrial decarbonization, and circular strategies scaled to maintain GDP growth while cutting emissions? If yes—and if these measures are credible and enforced—green growth becomes very likely. <cite id="67040153-2">Evidence from Israel shows that GDP growth and deep emissions cuts can be achieved simultaneously with credible policy standards and carbon pricing</cite> <cite id="67040153-0">Advanced economies would need to accelerate decarbonization several‑fold to align growth with 1.5 °C fair‑shares</cite>. Where these conditions are absent or partial, absolute decoupling remains out of reach; relative decoupling can occur but is not enough to meet climate targets. <cite id="67040153-4">Relative decoupling is common; absolute decoupling has not materialized at scale</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-3">Global scenarios converge that we are off‑track for 1.5/2 °C without faster, deeper mitigation</cite>.

Economic development has already started to decouple to some degree from production-or consumption-based emissions ( 12 -17 ), although with rates not fast enough to reach mitigation goals ( 18 ), fueling discussion on the feasibility of global-scale green growth with strong arguments for exploring scenarios with constant or even declining GDP in order to achieve such goals ( 19 -21 ). In line with this shift, certain cities are prioritizing social and environmental well-being over economic growth ( 22 , 23 ). 

Typically, studies on decoupling describe such developments at a global-scale using national data or focus on data from cities in specific countries. However, along with national commitments for climate mitigation, subnational climate action seems to be crucial for its success, with recent work in the US suggesting that subnational action alone could reduce total national emissions by between one quarter to a third ( 24 ). Notably, certain cities and subnational regions have already set independent climate mitigation or net-zero emission targets ( 25 -27 ). The advent of global data on subnational economic output ( 28 , 29 ) and carbon emissions ( 30 , 31 ) presents the opportunity for a global-scale analysis of emission decoupling with high granularity on a subnational level.

Title: Reconceptualizing Climate Change Denial: Ideological Denialism Misdiagnoses Climate Change and Limits Effective Action
Snippet: In recent decades many approaches to addressing environmental sustainability have centered on green growth. Aimed at meeting both economic and environmental goals simultaneously, green growth has emerged as a central framing in climate and broader environmental discourses (Hickel & Kallis, 2019). More specifically, green growth is often described as a win-win proposition-continuing economic growth while simultaneously meeting environmental outcomes and goals. In contrast to market fundamentalism (which represents a belief in the best mechanism to use), green growth (which could include market mechanisms) is a system in which proponents believe it is possible to address environmental harms while still growing the economy. Hallegatte et al. (2011, p. 3) explain succinctly: "green growth is about making growth processes resource-efficient, cleaner, and more resilient without necessarily slowing them," a seductive proposition but one that has many limitations and shortcomings. 

The promise of green growth relies on decoupling environmental harm from economic activity and growth. Theoretically possible, such decoupling has not yet materialized (Hickel & Kallis, 2019). Hickel and Kallis (2019) distinguish between relative and absolute decoupling. The former traces environmental impacts per unit of economic activity while the latter emphasizes overall reductions. Evidence exists to show relative decoupling, but not absolute (Schor & Jorgenson, 2019). Absolute decoupling has not occurred for many reasons. Green growth lends itself to GDP (gross domestic product) measures, a metric that inadequately addresses environmental outcomes and well-being. Green growth also relies heavily on technological advances but these often center on efficiency improvements, which the above discussion shows to be inadequate in terms of reducing material throughput. Proponents argue that decoupling will emerge as economies transition away from material-based economies to ones based on services, but dematerialization has not occurred (Hickel & Kallis, 2019). Lastly, evidence that developed nations have shown movement toward decoupling often fails to include the offshoring of emissions, those generated through shifting production to other countries (Hickel & Kallis, 2019).

Summary: Is green growth possible?
- Short answer: Yes—deep, sustained economic growth while sharply cutting emissions is technically feasible and is already occurring in parts of the economy, but only under strong, coordinated policy and structural change; present decarbonization rates in many advanced economies are still too slow to meet 1.5–2 °C targets while maintaining historical growth rates, so green growth pathways require faster power-sector decarbonization, electrification, circularity, and industrial process innovation, alongside robust carbon pricing and standards, and careful management of trade-offs and distributional issues. <cite id="67040153-0">Empirical studies show some high‑income countries have achieved absolute decoupling of emissions and GDP in the past decade, but current decoupling rates are insufficient to meet 1.5 °C fair‑share pathways while continuing historical GDP growth; for example, the UK would need to more than triple its decoupling rate by 2025 and accelerate it almost fivefold by 2030 to enable green growth consistent with a 1.5 °C budget</cite> <cite id="67040153-1">At the same time, observed subnational production decoupling remains inadequate for net‑zero by 2050, and scenarios that deliver green growth rely on rapid expansion of emissions‑free or negative‑emissions energy</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-3">Recent assessments find we are on a lower‑emissions trajectory than often assumed but are still off‑track for 1.5 °C or below 2 °C, implying that without faster mitigation, warming will be 2–3 °C by 2100</cite>.

What “green growth” means and what has been observed
- Definition and distinction: Green growth hinges on decoupling environmental pressures from economic activity. Evidence is strong for relative decoupling (emissions per unit of GDP down), but absolute decoupling (total emissions fall while GDP grows) has been rare and is the hard, contested target. <cite id="67040153-4">Theoretically, decoupling is possible; empirically, there is clear evidence for relative decoupling but not for absolute decoupling at national or global scales</cite> <cite id="67040153-3">Reviews conclude absolute long‑term decoupling of GDP and CO2 is rare; even when countries show decoupling in GDP–CO2, net resource/ material decoupling is not evident, and scholars argue 1.5–2 °C targets may not be feasible under continued growth without degrowth strategies</cite>.
- Real‑world achievements: Subnational jurisdictions and some advanced economies demonstrate partial/absolute decoupling in practice, often via energy intensity improvements, power sector decarbonization, and electrification. <cite id="67040153-1">Subnational action is crucial; in the US, subnational action alone could reduce national emissions by a quarter to a third, and many cities and regions have set independent net‑zero targets</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Model‑based assessments show absolute decoupling tendencies for highly industrialized economies (US, Germany, EU) under “climate‑active” baselines, though their per‑capita footprints remain high and global decoupling remains relative due to fast‑catching Asian economies</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">In Israel, GDP is projected to grow ~140% by 2050 under baseline, with energy‑related GHGs rising ~35%; with strong policy mixes, emissions can be reduced 40% (standards) to 67% (carbon pricing) relative to 2015, with power generation rising as electrification and solar scale</cite>.

How much faster must decarbonization proceed?
- Quantified gaps: Cross‑country analyses indicate current decoupling rates in advanced economies are inconsistent with fair‑share budgets under continued GDP growth. <cite id="67040153-0">Between 2013–2019, high‑income countries achieved decoupling but at rates far short of what is required to respect 1.5 °C carbon‑budget shares while maintaining historical GDP growth; the UK would need to increase its decoupling rate to 17.4% by 2025 (up from 5.3% per year) and to 23.9% by 2030—an acceleration by ~3–5×</cite>. 
- Global plausibility windows: Scenario frameworks from IPCC and modeling consortia show that low‑emission futures exist, but they require rapid, sustained mitigation beyond current policies. <cite id="9eb9de65-1">IPCC AR6 recognizes that scenarios with very high emissions (SSP5‑8.5/RCP8.5) are less likely, while low‑emission pathways (SSP1‑1.9) keep warming around 1.5 °C, reflecting feasibility of low‑growth or decoupled trajectories</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-3">A subset of plausible IPCC/IEA‑consistent scenarios projects 2–3 °C warming by 2100 with continued mitigation progress, indicating we are on a lower‑emissions path than commonly feared but still off‑track for 1.5/2 °C</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-0">Global cost‑optimal scenarios used by multiple IAMs underpin feasible pathways to below 1.5–2 °C when combined with socio‑economic assumptions across demographics, development, policy, technology, and natural resources</cite>.

Policy bundles that make green growth feasible
- Carbon pricing plus technology/standards: Deep cuts alongside continued GDP growth are achievable where carbon pricing is credible and paired with sectoral standards. <cite id="67040153-2">In Israel, a carbon tax alone reduces energy‑related GHGs by 67% versus baseline by 2050; technology standards add ~5% more reduction and induce higher power generation as transport electrifies and solar rises to ~65–85% of the mix in scenarios</cite>.
- Power sector decarbonization and electrification: The main engine of absolute decoupling in advanced economies. <cite id="58c13877-4">Decomposition shows that improvements in electricity intensity and shifts away from thermal generation were key drivers of emissions reductions in the US and Germany</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">EU, Germany, and the US exhibit absolute decoupling tendencies under climate‑active baselines, with strong reductions in per‑capita CO2 footprints while GDP grows</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">Electrification of transport and large shares of solar in the power mix are central to enabling GDP growth without emissions increases in high‑income contexts</cite>.
- Circular economy and material efficiency: Reducing material throughput is necessary to complement energy/efficiency decoupling. <cite id="58c13877-3">Model‑based assessments find that while advanced economies can achieve absolute decoupling tendencies, material footprint decoupling is weaker on average; China’s infrastructure investment dynamics drive relative global trends</cite> <cite id="67040153-3">Evidence reviews emphasize that effective resource use and emissions reduction are necessary for green growth, while absolute decoupling of GDP and material use remains rare; degrowth may be required where resource constraints bind</cite>.
- Trade‑offs and distribution: Green growth is not a free lunch; it involves short‑term costs and distributional challenges that can be addressed through just transition policies. <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Scholarship highlights that feasibility is multidimensional and that limited‑GDP‑energy growth pathways can reduce climate feasibility concerns, though they entail trade‑offs in social justice and energy system upskilling</cite>.

Constraints, critiques, and risks to feasibility
- Absolute vs relative decoupling and offshoring: Many economies have reduced emissions per unit GDP but not total emissions; trade and supply chains shift impacts without policy. <cite id="67040153-4">Evidence shows relative, not absolute, decoupling; offshoring and reliance on efficiency alone are major limits</cite> <cite id="67040153-3">Global reviews report no evidence of national/international net resource decoupling; dematerialization has not kept pace with GDP</cite>.
- Catch‑up dynamics in emerging economies: Rapid industrialization and infrastructure investment can keep material and emissions growth in lockstep with GDP, limiting global absolute decoupling. <cite id="58c13877-3">China’s surge in infrastructure investment sustains higher material footprints; relative global decoupling persists as Asian economies dominate material use growth</cite>.
- Rebound and behavioral limits: Even with efficiency gains, demand can rebound; technological progress often targets intensity rather than absolute throughput. <cite id="67040153-4">Critiques note that efficiency improvements are insufficient to reduce material throughput, and dematerialization has not materialized at scale</cite>.
- Scenario plausibility: Even with aggressive mitigation, plausible pathways still imply 2–3 °C without additional constraints, underscoring urgency. <cite id="9eb9de65-3">Plausible IPCC/IEA‑consistent scenarios project 2–3 °C by 2100 unless mitigation accelerates beyond current trajectories</cite>.

When is green growth “possible”?
- Technically possible with rapid, coordinated policy: Scenarios and case evidence show that sustained GDP growth with deep emissions cuts is feasible where carbon and non‑carbon prices internalize damages, where power supply rapidly decarbonizes, and where industry adopts process/technological innovations and circular practices. <cite id="67040153-1">Green growth is already embedded in many mitigation scenarios that project rising GDP with falling emissions via emission‑free or negative‑emissions energy</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">National case analysis demonstrates that GDP can grow while emissions are cut deeply when standards and carbon pricing are implemented</cite>.
- Politically and institutionally challenging: Feasibility depends on credible policy design and delivery across borders and supply chains. <cite id="67040153-0">Current decoupling rates in high‑income countries fall short of 1.5 °C fair‑shares at current GDP growth rates, implying policy must accelerate several‑fold within a decade</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Scholars argue mainstream IAMs may understate feasibility constraints, and lower‑growth pathways can reduce reliance on absolute decoupling and speed up renewable scaling</cite>.
- Resource and supply‑chain considerations: Critical minerals and manufacturing capacity for renewables/batteries/CCUS are bottlenecks that must be addressed in national industrial strategies. <cite id="58c13877-3">China’s dominance in infrastructure‑driven material footprints highlights the need to manage supply‑chain dependencies and accelerate raw‑material efficiency to enable global absolute decoupling</cite>.

What would make green growth more likely (conditions and steps)
- Price carbon comprehensively and credibly: High, rising carbon prices across fuels and products, paired with robust enforcement. <cite id="67040153-2">Carbon pricing alone can deliver −67% energy‑related GHG reductions versus baseline by 2050 in Israel, with sectoral standards adding further cuts</cite>.
- Electrify end‑uses and decarbonize power: Rapid expansion of variable renewables, grid modernization, long‑lived storage, and grid resilience; electrify transport, buildings, industry heat. <cite id="67040153-2">Electrification of transport and large solar shares in power mixes emerge endogenously in deep‑mitigation scenarios</cite> <cite id="58c13877-4">Improvements in electricity intensity and reductions in thermal generation share are key drivers of emissions reductions</cite>.
- Industrial decarbonization and circular economy: Process innovation, green steel/ hydrogen, CCUS where needed, industrial heat electrification, and circular design/lifecycle management. <cite id="58c13877-2">Manufacturing sector studies show large potential from technical progress and energy‑saving technologies; China’s scenarios suggest cost savings of $12–$35 billion by 2050 through CCS or hydrogen with energy efficiency</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Raw material intensity must decline to enable absolute decoupling at national level</cite>.
- Manage supply chains and trade: Address carbon leakage and embedded emissions via border‑adjustment and international standards; invest in clean supply‑chain capacity. <cite id="67040153-1">Subnational jurisdictions can materially cut national emissions, yet national policies remain essential to meet net‑zero targets</cite>.
- Finance and just transition: Redirect capital toward green assets; support workforce and community transitions. <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Limited GDP/energy growth pathways can reduce feasibility concerns of rapid mitigation but require careful attention to social and institutional feasibility</cite>.
- Monitor, audit, and adapt: Track absolute consumption‑based emissions, material footprints, and progress by geography and sector; close efficiency and offshoring gaps. <cite id="67040153-4">Accounting for offshored emissions is essential to assess true environmental impacts</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Decomposition of Kaya‑style identities highlights where to target efficiency, intensity, and structural change</cite>.

Bottom line
- Green growth is possible—economically, technically, and empirically—where policy creates strong price signals, invests in clean energy systems, and drives industrial and circular economy transformations. <cite id="67040153-1">Many mitigation scenarios assume GDP growth alongside emissions declines via emission‑free or negative‑emissions energy</cite> <cite id="67040153-2">National modeling shows GDP growth can proceed with emissions falling sharply when standards and carbon pricing are implemented</cite>. However, present trajectories in advanced economies are insufficient; without accelerating decarbonization several‑fold over the next decade, global warming will exceed 2 °C. <cite id="67040153-0">High‑income countries’ realized decoupling rates are far below what is needed to meet 1.5 °C fair‑share budgets while maintaining historical GDP growth</cite> <cite id="9eb9de65-3">Plausible IPCC/IEA‑consistent scenarios project 2–3 °C by 2100 unless mitigation accelerates</cite>. Making green growth the default, not an aspiration, requires credible carbon pricing, rapid power‑sector decarbonization, industrial process innovation, circular strategies, and governance that manages distributional and supply‑chain risks—conditions that are increasingly within reach but demand urgent, coordinated action. <cite id="9eb9de65-4">Scholarly debates emphasize feasibility is multidimensional and that limiting GDP/energy growth can reduce reliance on absolute decoupling and ease the pace of renewable upscaling</cite> <cite id="58c13877-3">Advanced economies can show absolute decoupling tendencies, but global absolute decoupling remains constrained by fast‑catching material use in Asia</cite>.

Uncertainties and where evidence is thin
- The magnitude of rebound effects and consumer behavior shifts varies by context and technology; better empirical identification is needed to calibrate policy packages. <cite id="67040153-4">Efficiency‑only strategies and service‑based economies are not sufficient to reduce material throughput</cite>.
- Critical mineral bottlenecks and geopolitical risks for clean tech supply chains remain under‑modeled in some national scenarios; more integrated supply‑chain and industrial policy evidence is needed. <cite id="58c13877-3">China’s infrastructure‑driven material footprints illustrate the sensitivity of decoupling to investment dynamics and supply‑chain control</cite>.

Title: Doing burden-sharing right to deliver natural climate solutions for carbon dioxide removal
Snippet: To cover a wide range of uncertainties, we set global carbon budget targets based on Energy and Agriculture, Forestry and Land-Use emissions of 32 shared socio-economic pathways (SSP) scenarios that keep global warming to below 1.5 • C (RCP 1.9) and 2 • C (RCP 2.6). Each SSP features distinguished characteristics in terms of demographic, human development, economic, lifestyle, policies, institutions, technology, environment, and natural resource, and use as input to model regions projections of economy, energy, land/natural resource, and emissions [32][33][34]. We exclude SSP3 scenarios as they are not feasible to generate lower than 2 • C warming by the end of 2100. The scenarios are derived from global cost-optimal scenarios [35] assessed by six different IAMs, namely AIM/CGE 2.0, GCAM 4.2, IMAGE 3.0.1, MESSAGE-GLOBIOM 1.0, REMIND-MAgPIE 1.5, and WITCH-GLOBIOM 3.1. There are four main Kyoto-GHGs (i.e. carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, including industrial F-gasses) that are included within this study. The emissions values follow the Global Warming Potential for a 100-year time horizon introduced in the Second Assessment Report of the IPCC and used under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Countries' gross domestic products (GDP) and population projections for these scenarios (income, in billion US$ adjusted to 2010 values) are obtained from the IIASA-SSP Database [36,37].

Title: Plausible 2005–2050 emissions scenarios project between 2 °C and 3 °C of warming by 2100
Snippet: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) uses carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions scenarios to imagine and evaluate 'a range of plausible futures, because human development is determined by a myriad of factors including human decision making' (IPCC WGIII 2014a, p 48). Scenarios used in the IPCC 5th Assessment Reports (AR5) (IPCC 2014) and 6th Assessment Reports (AR6; IPCC 2021) include the 'Representative Concentration Pathways' (RCPs) and the 'Shared Socioeconomic Pathways' (SSPs) (Moss et al 2010, Riahi et al 2017). The high-emissions end of the RCP/SSP range is consistent with 8.5 W m −2 radiative forcing and 4 • C-5 • C of warming relative to pre-industrial levels by 2100 (e.g. SSP5-8.5, RCP8.5) (Hausfather and Peters 2020a). A system can easily retrieve optimistic and pessimistic papers and summarize both positions. Making it harder: (1) Could embed a false premise, but 'green growth' itself is a legitimate contested concept. (2) Could ask for reconciliation of conflicting evidence, but the field already explicitly debates this—papers frame themselves as pro/con decoupling, so retrieving both sides is straightforward. (3) Could demand a specific threshold (e.g., 'sufficient to meet Paris targets'), but empirical threshold claims appear directly in papers. (4) A stronger option: exploit that the debate conflates RELATIVE vs ABSOLUTE decoupling, and conflates PAST TRENDS vs FUTURE PROJECTIONS. A system can retrieve papers showing 'some countries achieved relative decoupling' and 'absolute decoupling is projected under policy X' without catching that past relative ≠ future absolute, which is a reasoning distinction not retrieval. (5) Even stronger: embed a constraint requiring the answer to hold CONDITIONAL on a specific policy regime the literature doesn't neatly isolate—force evaluation under assumptions that cross-cut existing studies. Best strategy: require conditional reasoning on an assumption (steady energy demand growth) that inverts the usual framing, making most retrieved evidence inapplicable without transformation.

This is a reasoning transformation, not retrieval—the literature doesn't frame answers conditional on this specific demand trajectory.

Summary
Green growth while global energy demand grows at 3% per year through 2050 is technically feasible if accompanied by rapid decarbonization of supply and end uses, massive clean energy deployment, and deep system upgrades, but it is very tight on the margin. Net‑zero pathways show that emissions can be driven to near zero by shifting most electricity to wind/solar/nuclear, electrifying buildings, transport, and industry, and deploying large‑scale CCS and hydrogen where hard‑to‑abate sectors remain. Many such pathways achieve ~80–90% low‑carbon electricity by mid‑century and hundreds of terawatts of cumulative clean capacity, while some allow modest net energy demand growth and others require declines; sustaining 3% per‑year growth through 2050 generally implies net‑zero electricity and sectoral electrification at very high scale and significant balancing/infrastructure investments. <cite id="252f9b10-0">Net zero energy sector pathways require electricity to supply ~88% of energy demand by 2050, with fossil fuels falling to about one‑fifth of supply, energy intensity improvements averaging 4% per year to 2030, and investments more than doubling to ~$5 trillion per year by 2030</cite> <cite id="252f9b10-1">Global energy consumption could rise by up to 50% by 2050, with uneven spatial demand growth and infrastructure and regulatory barriers to clean adoption</cite> <cite id="2a659477-1">Under IEA net‑zero, global electricity supply must reach ~50% of total energy by 2050, with ~88% of electricity from wind and solar, implying sustained wind additions of ~390 GW per year by 2030 (rising to ~8,000 GW by 2050)</cite> <cite id="e9676831-0">Across EMF‑37 net‑zero scenarios, end‑use electrification rises to an average of 43% by 2050 (74% buildings, 32% industry, 31% transport), with steeper increases relative to a business‑as‑usual case</cite> <cite id="e9676831-4">Buildings electrification can surpass 90% in many models by 2050, while transport may reach 40–80% and industry stabilize below 40%, shaping future electricity demand</cite>.

What net‑zero pathways imply about growth and feasibility
Net‑zero emissions by 2050 requires deep structural change: shifting most final energy to low‑carbon electricity, massive clean energy build‑out, and large‑scale electrification across sectors. <cite id="252f9b10-0">The IEA net‑zero pathway assumes the world economy in 2030 is 2/5 larger but uses 7% less energy than 2020, requiring average energy intensity improvements of 4% per year to 2030 (roughly 3× the pace achieved over the last two decades), shrinking fossil fuels to ~20% of energy supply by 2050, and cutting global energy demand by 8% by 2050 relative to 2020 in the net‑zero scenario</cite>. <cite id="e9676831-0">Net‑zero scenarios show steeper electrification than business‑as‑usual by 2050 (buildings ~74% electrified, industry ~32%, transport ~31%), with increased electricity share in final energy averaging 43% across sectors</cite>. These pathways demonstrate that both supply and demand can be transformed rapidly: <cite id="2a659477-1">wind capacity additions must average ~390 GW per year by 2030 in an IEA net‑zero case, yielding ~8,000 GW by 2050 (88% of electricity from wind and solar), and electricity supply rises to ~50% of energy and ~21 GtCO2 emissions in 2030 before reaching net‑zero by 2050</cite>. <cite id="e9676831-4">Buildings are the largest electricity consumers (75% of total electricity in 2020), with projected building electrification 55–100% by 2050; industry starts from <20% electrified today and rises but remains below ~40% electrification share; transport starts near 1% electrified and rises to ~40–80% across models</cite>.

Can 3% per‑year energy demand growth through 2050 be “green”?
Feasibility hinges on three levers: (1) very rapid decarbonization of supply, (2) deep electrification of end uses, and (3) system‑level balancing and infrastructure at planetary scale. <cite id="2a659477-1">To reach net‑zero CO2 emissions by 2050, global energy‑related and industrial process CO2 emissions must fall to ~21 Gt in 2030 and net‑zero in 2050, with ~50% of energy supply in electricity and 88% of that from wind and solar, requiring sustained additions of ~390 GW of wind per year by 2030 and cumulative capacity near ~8,000 GW by 2050</cite>. <cite id="e9676831-0">Net‑zero scenarios demonstrate that electricity can supply ~40% of final energy by 2050 on average (74% in buildings, 32% in industry, 31% in transport), implying that final energy demand may grow or shrink depending on the balance of efficiency and electrification</cite>. Thus, sustaining 3% annual energy demand growth through 2050 is compatible with green growth if:
- Carbon intensity of supply drops steeply: <cite id="252f9b10-0">fossil fuels fall to ~20% of total energy supply by 2050 and energy intensity improves by ~4%/year to 2030</cite>, and <cite id="2a659477-1">~88% of electricity is wind/solar</cite>.
- End‑use electrification offsets demand growth: <cite id="e9676831-0">Electrification increases by 10–13 percentage points across sectors relative to business‑as‑usual, with larger gains in transport and buildings</cite> and <cite id="e9676831-4">buildings and transport reach high electrification shares, while industry rises but remains constrained</cite>.
- System upgrades are provided at speed and scale: <cite id="252f9b10-0">Investments must more than double to ~$5 trillion/year by 2030</cite>; <cite id="b676261c-0">CCS capacity must grow by roughly an order of magnitude, reaching 1.6 GtCO2 by 2030 and ~7.6 GtCO2 by 2050 in IEA’s Net Zero case</cite>; and <cite id="b676261c-2">hydrogen can supply ~0.8–2% of global energy by 2050, with transport and city gas as major end uses, but requires CCS or low‑carbon power when scaled</cite>.

Evidence from sectoral transformations shows that 3% growth is plausible within net‑zero constraints if hard‑to‑electrify sectors are supplied by low‑carbon hydrogen and CCS. <cite id="e9676831-3">In U.S. models, industry electrification can rise to ~29–30% by 2050 in net‑zero scenarios, with emissions pressure mitigated by electrification in transportation and buildings</cite>. <cite id="e9676831-2">China’s carbon‑neutral vision shows that electrification in buildings can peak and then slightly decline while remaining ~80% electrified in end use, and transport demand grows rapidly but becomes more efficient with EVs; industry decarbonization relies on CCS and H2‑DRI/steel and cement with large CO2 reductions</cite>. <cite id="b676261c-1">When hydrogen is used extensively, total electricity demand can be ~5× higher in 1.5 °C cases, requiring >7,000 GW of renewable power, with the chemical/petrochemical sector relying on CCS and contributing ~25% of global CCS use</cite>. What makes 3% growth “safe”?
A 3% annual energy demand growth through 2050 can be “green” if it operates within net‑zero pathways’ envelopes—i.e., emissions intensity approaches zero, end‑use electrification is deep, and supply and system upgrades scale rapidly. <cite id="252f9b10-0">Policy packages that deliver 4% per‑year energy‑intensity improvement to 2030, a collapse of fossil shares to ~20% by 2050, and $5+ trillion/year in clean energy investment</cite> combined with <cite id="2a659477-1">~50% low‑carbon electricity by 2050 (88% wind/solar), sustained wind additions of ~390 GW/year by 2030, and cumulative capacity near ~8,000 GW by 2050</cite> and <cite id="e9676831-0">~43% end‑use electrification on average by 2050 (74% buildings, 32% industry, 31% transport)</cite> would keep net emissions in check even with ~3% energy growth. - 3% annual energy demand growth to 2050 is compatible with “green growth” if embedded within such net‑zero trajectories, driven by very low‑carbon electricity, deep electrification in buildings and transport, and large‑scale H2/CCS in hard‑to‑electrify industrial uses, backed by extensive grid, storage, and interconnection investments. <cite id="e9676831-0">Electrification increases by 10–13 percentage points across sectors relative to business‑as‑usual in net‑zero scenarios</cite> and <cite id="e9676831-4">buildings and transport reach high electrification shares while industry rises but remains constrained</cite>, while <cite id="b676261c-0">CCS capacity must expand by two orders of magnitude</cite> and <cite id="b676261c-2">hydrogen can supply ~1% of global energy by 2050 when paired with low‑carbon power or CCS</cite>.

Thus, “green” 3% growth requires policy, investment, and technological execution that are aggressive by historical standards.

Practical implications

The central risk is under‑investment or policy reversal that keeps carbon intensity high; with strong governance, 3% growth can ride the green wave rather than drive warming. </answer>

Title: The Role of Trade in Asia and the Pacific’s Net Zero Pathways: Overview and Policy Implications
Snippet: The International Energy Agency (IEA 2021) conducted a comprehensive study on the net zero transition for the energy sector, which accounts for three-fourths of greenhouse gases. The influential study put forward three main scenarios: (i) Stated Policy Scenario, including specific plans already in place or announced by governments; (ii) Announcement Pledges Case, where all announced national zero pledges were assumed to be achieved on time; and (iii) Net Zero Scenario by 2050, which forms the core of the analysis in the paper. The Stated Policy Scenario would lead global temperatures to rise 2.7°C, while the rise in the Pledges Case scenarios would be 2.1°C (each with a 50% probability). Net zero would be consistent with a 1.5°C rise (with a 50% probability). 

The study's net zero scenario stipulates the necessary conditions for the global energy sector to reach net zero emissions by 2050. 17 The policy challenges are daunting. The net zero pathway assumes the world economy in 2030 will be two-fifths larger than today but will use 7% less energy, requiring an energy intensity improvement of 4% per year on average to 2030, or about 3 times that achieved over the past 2 decades. It will require a major increase in renewable energy use, energy efficiency, and clean energy innovations, while fossil fuels will have to shrink to about one-fifth of the energy supply by 2050, from about four-fifths today. Moreover, the net zero scenario requires that global energy demand by 2050 fall by 8%, posing a considerable challenge with 2 billion additional people on the planet. Emissions from industry, transport, and buildings will have to fall by 95% by 2050, requiring major efforts to build new and retool existing infrastructure. 

Investments associated with the shift toward net zero are massive. 

The IEA study uses modeling undertaken with the International Monetary Fund to calculate annual investment requirements for the energy sector. It concludes that such investments will need to more than double to $5 trillion by 2030, from about $2.3 trillion currently. On the positive side, this should add 0.4% to annual global GDP growth.

Title: When Cities Go Nuclear: Exploring the Applications of Nuclear Batteries Toward Energy Transformation
Snippet: By 2050, global energy consumption could increase by up to 50% [1]. Energy demand will be driven by global population growth, increasing access to electricity, rising incomes, and urbanization [1]. This demand will be spatially unevenly distributed, with accelerating urbanization happening in the global south, and the industrial hinterland feeding their appetites for food, water, fuel, data, and other resources. Manufacturing, materials processing, transportation, and buildings are already responsible for over 80% of global carbon emissions [2]. 

Fossil fuels continue to dominate the energy market, producing more than 80% of global energy [3]. The projected growth in energy demand over the next 30 years will occur in regions heavily reliant on CO 2 -emitting energy sources [1] The International Energy Agency [4] has set the imperative of transitioning to net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 to avert the worst effects of climate change. 

Renewable energy sources are the fastest-growing segment of the energy sector [1]. The global installed capacity of renewable energy reached 2537 GW at the end of 2019, with hydropower leading the way (1190 GW globally), followed by wind energy (623 GW), and solar (586 GW) [5]. Explaining the simultaneous growth in demand for fossil fuels and growth in renewable energy adoption is a daunting cost differential; the overhead of capital required to begin renewable energy projects has been cited extensively as a barrier to renewable energy adoption, though the cost of clean energy relative to traditional energy has diminished substantially in recent years. Now, the overestimation of risk by financial institutions, the lack of legal and regulatory frameworks, and limitations on existing infrastructure and skills hinder the deployment of clean energy [6]. To achieve the deep decarbonization required to address these issues on a planetary scale, it is necessary to integrate low-carbon energy solutions into every sector of the economy while addressing the unprecedented need for speed and scaling, while balancing security, affordability, and sustainability [9].

Title: The unequivocal case for net zero green growth
Snippet: This paper makes the case for net zero (or, more broadly, green) growth. It argues that net zero green growth is the most realistic strategy for halting global warming and meeting the objectives of the Paris Agreement. Net zero growth is feasible technologically, economically and behaviourally. Credible decarbonisation paths have been modelled and the leading countries have already broken the link between emissions and gross domestic product. Green growth, which emphasises economic opportunities, is the best way to mobilise the clean innovation and investment that net zero requires, and it is the best strategy to secure public support for rapid decarbonisation.

Title: Trading Off Global Fuel Supply, CO2 Emissions and Sustainable Development
Snippet: The global economic growth rate (3.9%±1.4%yr -  since 1950) [27] has only dropped below 2% during major recessions. This growth rate profile resulted in an average annual increase in energy use of 2.17% person -1 (Fig 1B green). In comparison, global energy efficiency savings have been significantly lower (0.61%yr -1 ). This is consistent with the IEA technology perspectives report which concluded that the OECD 11 countries have achieved annual energy efficiency improvements of 0.7% since 1973 [3]. To improve upon this, the International Energy Agency has proposed a 'Blue Map Target' with an additional 0.8% yr -1 energy savings from 2011, yielding 1.41% savings in total [3]. But the rate of increase in energy use (2.17% person -1 yr -1 ) remains significantly higher than any of the above energy saving scenarios (0%, 0.61% or 1.41%). Conversely, a growth in energy demand which matches either observed or aspirational energy efficiency gains, necessarily requires significantly lower GDP growth than historical averages. We conclude that energy demand will most likely continue to rise even in the face of modest GDP per capita growth. The forecast global population increase from ~7 billion in 2008 to ~9 billion people by 2050 and possibly to 14 billion by 2100, compounds this problem and will likely have serious implications for economic, energy and climate change policy even if the additional population lives in poverty and uses little energy. As expected, varying the economic growth rate (Fig 2A curves 4 (2.5%), 3 (3.9%) and 2 (5.3%) yr -1 GDP) did not significantly alter energy efficiency improvements between 2010-2050 (37.5%, 38% and 38.2% respectively) in terms of ZJ GDP -1 , further validating the model in Eq 1.

Title: Impact of financial development on the energy intensity of developing countries
Snippet: The 2050 net-zero emissions target refers to the plan to reduce global carbon dioxide emissions to net zero by 2050. The energy sector is the source of about three-quarters of today's greenhouse gas emissions. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), reducing these emissions is both the key to achieving net zero emissions by 2050 and the greatest challenge facing humanity. Thus, energy consumption and energy intensity have always been a focus. Energy consumption is directly proportional to carbon emissions (Shahbaz et al., 2018). The decrease in the growth rate of energy consumption benefits from the reduction of energy intensity. Furthermore, in order to lower energy intensity, it is critical to investigate the elements that influence it. According to BP (British Petroleum), world energy consumption rose 1.3% in 2019 over the prior year, below the 10-year average of 1.6% growth and well below the 2.8% growth rate recorded in 2018. Carbon emissions grew by 0.5% in 2019, which, while lower than the average growth rate of 1.1% over the past decade and below the 2.1% growth rate in 2018, only partially hedged the substantial growth in 2018 (BP, 2020). Global energy intensity decreased by 2% in 2019, and by only 1.6% when weather was taken into account, roughly the same as in 2018. However, this improvement is well below the average between 2010 and 2017, and well below the 3.6% standard required to achieve the IEA's Sustainable Development Scenario (SDS) in 2020-2040(IEA, 2020)). 

Regionally, almost all advanced economies have experienced a decline in energy demand, with a total decline of 1% in 2019, led by the European Union (2%) and the United States (0.8%). While developing countries have continued to increase their energy demand, China accounted for a staggering 90% of the net growth in global energy demand in 2019. Southeast Asia's energy demand grew strongly, at 3.4% in 2019. The decline in aggregate energy demand in advanced economies is directly due to improvements in energy efficiency, followed by indirect efficiency gains due to a shift to low-carbon energy sources with lower generation losses (IEA, 2020).

Title: The Role of Trade in Asia and the Pacific’s Net Zero Pathways: Overview and Policy Implications
Snippet: The International Energy Agency (IEA 2021) conducted a comprehensive study on the net zero transition for the energy sector, which accounts for three-fourths of greenhouse gases. The influential study put forward three main scenarios: (i) Stated Policy Scenario, including specific plans already in place or announced by governments; (ii) Announcement Pledges Case, where all announced national zero pledges were assumed to be achieved on time; and (iii) Net Zero Scenario by 2050, which forms the core of the analysis in the paper. The Stated Policy Scenario would lead global temperatures to rise 2.7°C, while the rise in the Pledges Case scenarios would be 2.1°C (each with a 50% probability). Net zero would be consistent with a 1.5°C rise (with a 50% probability). 

The study's net zero scenario stipulates the necessary conditions for the global energy sector to reach net zero emissions by 2050. 17 The policy challenges are daunting. The net zero pathway assumes the world economy in 2030 will be two-fifths larger than today but will use 7% less energy, requiring an energy intensity improvement of 4% per year on average to 2030, or about 3 times that achieved over the past 2 decades. It will require a major increase in renewable energy use, energy efficiency, and clean energy innovations, while fossil fuels will have to shrink to about one-fifth of the energy supply by 2050, from about four-fifths today. Moreover, the net zero scenario requires that global energy demand by 2050 fall by 8%, posing a considerable challenge with 2 billion additional people on the planet. Emissions from industry, transport, and buildings will have to fall by 95% by 2050, requiring major efforts to build new and retool existing infrastructure. 

Investments associated with the shift toward net zero are massive. 

The IEA study uses modeling undertaken with the International Monetary Fund to calculate annual investment requirements for the energy sector. It concludes that such investments will need to more than double to $5 trillion by 2030, from about $2.3 trillion currently. On the positive side, this should add 0.4% to annual global GDP growth.
